lines.note: Continues keage from the preceding page with water and dust as objects raised by a kick. Mari wo ke aguru introduces kicking a ball upward; the printed space in qe agu- is retained.

runs.text: Lançar pera cima a pella com o pè.

lines.note: Completes aguru and explains sending the ball upward with the foot. This confirms that the preceding page's como was a catchword, not an extra body line.

runs.text: Pelejar dando com os pees de

lines.note: Keai describes fighting by kicking. The contracted principal forms with caroned o are printed explicitly and are not replaced with modern forms.
Specifies spurring or kicking as cocks do in a fight. This completes keai before a separate causative entry omitted by OCR.
Keawase is making cocks fight. This complete physical row was missing from the provisional Markdown; it has been inserted under a fresh ID without renumbering later rows, with its own verified crop.

runs.text: O amarrar, ou liar. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: Kebaku means binding or tying. The dictionary then introduces a figurative application rather than a second literal tying action.
Toga ni kebaku seraruru means being bound by faults or sins. The passive construction corresponds to the Portuguese ser preso.
Completes the explanation of being tied by sins. This is the figurative use announced above.

runs.text: Tomar o Fotoque outra figura, & no-

lines.note: Kebut describes a Buddha taking another form and name. Fotoque is embedded within the Portuguese explanation; the bare final t in the headword is retained.

runs.text: me diferente do primeiro com que ſe tinha ma-

lines.note: Completes nome and specifies a form or name different from the first manifestation. The scan supports diferente with f, not the OCR's meaning-distorting long-s reading diſerente.
Completes manifestado and the account of an earlier manifestation. The source's physical division and short-s spelling are preserved.

runs.text: O por ouro nos veſtidos de ſeda, ou

lines.note: Kekake here denotes applying gold to silk clothing or girdles. This nominal craft term is distinct from the kicking verb with the same spelling below.
Specifies gold applied among the painted or worked designs on girdles. The Portuguese cingidouros and lauores retain their printed historical forms.
Gives a kekake obi or kosode as examples of the gilded work. The Latin l marks alternatives, while Cingi- begins the Portuguese description of a girdle.

runs.text: douro, ou veſtido de ſeda dourado, & pinta-

lines.note: Completes cingidouro and describes a gilded and painted silk garment. Pinta- is continued below as part of the same description.
Completes pintado and refers back to the stated gilding technique. This closes the craft sense of qecaqe.
Kekake as a verb means throwing or splashing something with the foot. The following examples identify the material kicked.

runs.text: pee como agoa, ou lama. Vt,

lines.note: Gives water or mud as examples, with the Japanese alternatives doro and mizu. The form mizzu is preserved rather than modernized.

runs.text: Deitar com o pee lama, ou

lines.note: Completes doro or mizu wo kekakuru, casting mud or water with the foot. The scan reads pee with two e types; the draft lost the second e in this occurrence.
Completes the example with water as the alternative to mud. This ends the kicking-and-splashing entry.
Kekachi denotes general famine or barrenness. The visibly unusual accent in gèral and the historical spelling esterilidade are retained.

Kekkai is paraphrased by isagiyoi and imashime, a pure or good prohibition. The Portuguese introduces a law or prohibition. The open c-like glyph in cu is retained literally; ou is the expected conjunction, but a worn o cannot be distinguished with certainty from an actual c.
Completes prohibição and characterizes it as pure and good. This explains the two Japanese paraphrase elements above.
Kekkō is paraphrased with tying or arranging, and glossed as preparing or equipping. The headword has a circumflex over o in this occurrence.
Continues the preparation sense and begins mono wo kekkō suru, arranging or preparing something. The Japanese example continues below.
Completes mono wo kekkō suru, then adds good arrangement and ornament as another sense. The right-edge ampersand is visible and retained, with the crop including the adjacent rule.
Completes the description of a well-arranged, ornamented, fine and lustrous thing. This leads naturally into the adjective entry below.

runs.text: Couſa excelente, ou fermoſa, bẽ cõ-

lines.note: Kekkō na describes something excellent, beautiful, or well arranged. The scan has a circumflex, not the draft's caron; bẽ and cõ- preserve nasal abbreviations.
Completes concertada, well arranged or finished. This is the last part of the adjective gloss.
Gives the adverbial form kekkō ni, associated by indentation with the adjective above. No separate Portuguese definition is printed.
Gives the -sa nominal form, the quality of excellence or fine arrangement. The circumflex and long s remain literal.
Kekku is glossed as rather or on the contrary. The scan shows two l types in pollo, which the draft reduced to one.
Kechaku is paraphrased as the household's heir, ie no chakushi. The initial capital is Q, not OCR D; the Portuguese morgado supplies the heir or entail sense.

runs.text: Prenoſtico de algũa couſa em mà par-

lines.note: Kechi denotes an unfavorable omen. The Portuguese specifies a bad interpretation, with par- continuing below.
Completes em mà parte and gives kechi ga aru or dekita, an omen existing or occurring. The two examples are alternatives introduced by l.

runs.text: ou ter acõtecido algũa couſa de ruim prenoſtico.

lines.note: Explains having experienced something of bad omen. The nasal abbreviation in acõtecido remains unexpanded.
Kechigiri means snapping a thread or cord with the foot. The double t in itta belongs to the printed principal-part pattern.
Completes corda and specifies the foot as the means of breaking it. The doubled vowel in pee is retained.
Kechimyaku is referred to the preferred form Qetmiacu. Meliùs and Vide are italic editorial apparatus, while the referenced Japanese headword is upright.
Infrà tells the reader to look below for the preferred headword. Its grave accent is preserved.
Kechirakashi means scattering something by kicking. The following row supplies the means, and the historical aita inflection is retained.
Completes the scattering definition with the foot as the instrument. It belongs to kechirakashi, before the preferred shorter verb below.
Kechirashi is marked as the better form with the same meaning. The lexical preference is the dictionary's own, not an editorial modernization.

runs.text: Eſmola, ou obra pia que hum faz

lines.note: Kechien is explained as almsgiving or a pious action. The following rows connect it with salvation and earning merit.

runs.text: com intento deſe ſaluar, & ganhar merecimẽto.

lines.note: Describes performing the action to obtain salvation and merit. The nasal abbreviation in merecimẽto is preserved.
Kechien suru means giving alms or doing pious works. The paragraph marker is present in the scan but missing from the draft; o- begins obras below.
Completes obras pias, then gives kechien ni azukaru, receiving the benefit of alms or mercy. The scan reads azzucaru with c, not OCR azzutaru; Re- continues at the top of column 2.
Completes receber, receiving alms or mercy, and introduces another sense of kechien. This row continues the entry across the column boundary.

runs.text: Merecimento, ou retribuição que hum eſpera na

lines.note: Defines the further sense as merit or a recompense one expects. The time or realm of that reward is given on the next row.
The reward is expected in the other life. Kechien ni naru introduces being meritorious; the alternative example begins qe- and continues on the next physical row.
Completes the alternative kechien de gozaru. The Portuguese equates it with being meritorious or being a work worthy of reward, not merely with receiving material alms.

runs.text: digna deſer galardoada na outra vida.

lines.note: Finishes the merit definition with a work deserving reward in the other life. The printed joining deſer is retained rather than silently respaced.
Kekorobakashi is to knock something down by kicking. The means and direction follow below; the historical verb ending aita is preserved.
Specifies using the foot in a forward direction. This continuation belongs to the verb above, not to the architectural noun beginning on the next row.

runs.text: Hũs paos como ti ãtes, ou colũ-

lines.note: Kekorobashi names pieces of wood likened to tie-beams or small posts. The scan visibly has ti ãtes, with a gap where tirãtes would normally have r, and ends colũ- before pequenas below. Both defective-looking printed forms are retained; neither an r nor a missing continuation nas is supplied without visible type.

Pequenas completes the description of small posts at the left. The parenthesis and pera diante are physically displaced at the far right, apparently supplementing the killing-by-kicking definition on the next row; their actual placement is encoded rather than merging them into the post definition.
Kekoroshi is killing by a kick. The printed principal part is roita and is not modernized; the adjacent displaced pera diante is retained on its own physical row above.

Kekke denotes a reckoning or computation, with kekke suru as the example. The damaged word reads computaçaõ, not compuiaçaõ: the t and the nasal mark on the final o are visible. The joined example Qecqeſuru follows the printed spacing.
Kekki is the vigour of the blood. This is a new headword at the entry margin, so the draft's continuation indentation is removed; sa- begins the following Japanese predicate.

runs.text: Eſtar o ſangue em ſeu vigor.

lines.note: Completes kekki sakan na, the blood being in full vigour. The physical sa-/can division is preserved, without imposing modern word boundaries.

Kekkwan is exemplified by the printed Qecquan chǒnin and explained below as deprivation of offices and dignities. Vt is one italic Latin abbreviation, not a roman V followed by italic t; the Japanese example remains roman.

runs.text: ſer priuado de officios, & dignidades, ou bor-

lines.note: Defines loss of offices and dignities, then starts borrado. The historical spelling officios and the line-final division bor- are retained.

runs.text: rado do rol, & liuro deſtas dignidades, que

lines.note: Completes borrado and explains removal from the roll or book of those dignities. The relative clause naming the authority continues on the next row.

The Dayri is the authority who grants or withdraws the dignities. Dayri is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese prose and is therefore flagged for whole-word typeface review; the printed grave in dà is retained.
Kekuzushi means destroying or breaking something apart with the feet. The doubled zz in the historical spelling and the nasal abbreviation in deſmã- are both present in the scan.
Completes desmanchar and specifies the feet as the means of destruction. The plural pees is retained, rather than replacing it with a modern accented form.
Kedai is glossed by okotari/okotaru and by fault or neglect. The Portuguese c in deſcui- has no cedilla in the scan; the draft's deſçui- is corrected without changing the historical Japanese forms.

runs.text: do, ou priguiça em fazer executar algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes descuido and adds laziness in carrying something out. The printed priguiça, rather than modern preguiça, and the nasal abbreviation algũa are retained.
Kedai wo suru means failing or being lazy. The paragraph marker is clearly printed at the left of the example and is restored from the scan.
Kedai-gachi is repeated or habitual neglect. The Portuguese explicitly says many times, matching the habitual tendency conveyed by the Japanese form.
The example describes a person prone to neglect or failure. The paragraph marker and the ligature in Peßoa are retained, with the Japanese example set in roman type.
Completes the description of someone repeatedly neglectful. This row finishes the example above and does not introduce a separate headword.
Kedamono is defined here as a four-footed animal. The unaccented historical plural pees is the printed form.

Kedashi is an adverb of possibility or qualification, rendered by Poruentura and ſaluoſe. The draft's internal gap in ſa luoſe is not a word boundary in the scan and is removed; the final register abbreviation S. remains as printed.
Keden denotes sudden fright or astonishment. Its suru example is printed continuously and divided after ſu- at the right edge.
Completes Qedenſuru and translates it as being suddenly frightened. The unaccented printed ſubito is retained.

The Japanese gloss describes teaching the path of salvation, matching the Portuguese continuation. Qedǒ has a caron-shaped long-vowel sign in the scan, unlike the unmarked Qedo headword two rows below.

runs.text: nar a ſaluação, ou guiar no caminho da ſaluação.

lines.note: Completes ensinar and paraphrases the action as guiding someone on the path of salvation. The two occurrences of ſaluação retain their printed nasal marks.
Qedo is glossed as tasukuru koto, saving, with a human-object example following. The synonym after i, is an ordinary Japanese gloss, not a Japanese word embedded inside Portuguese prose.
Hito wo qedo suru is translated as saving people. The nasal abbreviation in homẽs is visible and retained.
Kehanachi is putting or pushing something away with the foot. The historical tçu/atta principal parts and the nasal abbreviation cõ are preserved.
Specifies the foot, then begins an example about kicking away the left stirrup. The sign on pè is a grave accent, not the nasal mark represented by the draft's pẽ.
The example continues with falling suddenly to the right. Yax. is the printed citation label and is flagged for whole-word typeface review; Afas- begins the Portuguese explanation below.

runs.text: tando com o pè o estribo eſquerdo, deu conſigo

lines.note: Completes afastando and explains kicking aside the left stirrup before falling. Both the grave-accented pè and the historical spelling eſquerdo are retained.
Finishes the quoted action with falling to the ground on the right-hand side. The printed joining aparte is preserved rather than normalizing it to a parte.

runs.text: Couſa crdinaria como veſtido que ſe

lines.note: Ke and hare contrast ordinary and special-occasion use, here illustrated by clothing. The first glyph of crdinaria is visibly open and c-like, as in cu on c1-l021; that literal reading is retained rather than silently emending to ordinaria. A worn o remains possible.

runs.text: traz de còte, & extraordinaria como veſtido,

lines.note: The contrast is between clothing worn daily and extraordinary or special-occasion clothing. The phrase de còte retains its visible grave accent.

runs.text: ou trajo que ſe traz por festa, ou em publico.

lines.note: Continues with dress worn for a festival or in public. The verb is traz with lowercase t, not the draft's capital Iraz; the unaccented publico follows the print.
The example ke hare no ishō refers to clothing of the two kinds. The worn medial letter is x, not OCR t, giving the familiar Jesuit spelling ixǒ; the long-vowel sign is retained.
Completes destas layas, then gives ke hare wo suru as using the appropriate clothing or equipment. The paragraph marker separates the example without starting a new physical row.

runs.text: vestidos, ou aparelhos ordinarios, & de feſta

lines.note: Names ordinary and festive clothing or equipment. Vestidos contains visible st, not the draft's vesidos; the two s forms elsewhere on the row are preserved as they appear in the type.
Concludes that each kind is used at its proper time. This short continuation remains attached physically to the clothing discussion, before the armour-lacing headword.
Kebiki describes threads or straps woven and linked through armour plates. The scan's headword is Qefiqi, with historical f, and encadea- continues on the next row.
Completes encadeadas and locates the lacing in the plates of armour. The signature and catchword below are page furniture, not a further body line of this definition.
